# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Block Diagram — BPF Realization (Cascade Method)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Input Signal Vi] --> B[Stage 1: First Order HPF R1C1]
    B --> C[Buffer / Voltage Follower OpAmp]
    C --> D[Stage 2: First Order LPF R2C2]
    D --> E[Output Vo = Band Passed Signal]
    F[fL set by R1C1] -.-> B
    G[fH set by R2C2] -.-> D
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Read the diagram left-to-right:** The input signal first encounters the HPF, which removes low-frequency content. The buffered signal then enters the LPF, which removes high-frequency content. The final output contains only the **band** between $f_L$ and $f_H$.

## 4.2 Block Diagram — Wide-Band BRF Realization (Parallel / Summation Method)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Input Signal Vi] --> B[Input Splitter / Buffer]
    B --> C1[Upper Path: LPF R2C2]
    B --> C2[Lower Path: HPF R1C1]
    C1 --> D[Summing Amplifier or Node]
    C2 --> D
    D --> E[Output Vo = Band Rejected Signal]
    F[Passes f below fL] -.-> C1
    G[Passes f above fH] -.-> C2
    H[Rejects f between fL and fH] -.-> D
```

> [!TIP]
> **Why Parallel?** Notice that in the BRF case, the two filter paths operate in **parallel** (not in series) because we need to **preserve** the low and high frequencies, and only the middle band should be cancelled. The LPF and HPF outputs are **added** algebraically at the summing node.

## 4.3 Frequency Response Characteristics (Conceptual Mermaid Plot)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph BPF_Response["BAND PASS FILTER RESPONSE"]
        direction LR
        P1[Low Freq Rejected] --> P2[Gain Rises at fL]
        P2 --> P3[Peak Gain at f0]
        P3 --> P4[Gain Falls at fH]
        P4 --> P5[High Freq Rejected]
    end
    subgraph BRF_Response["BAND REJECTION FILTER RESPONSE"]
        direction LR
        Q1[Low Freq Passed] --> Q2[Gain Steady till fL]
        Q2 --> Q3[Notch Dip at f0]
        Q3 --> Q4[Gain Rises at fH]
        Q4 --> Q5[High Freq Passed]
    end
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Visual Distinction:** In a **BPF**, the curve is a **bell shape** (peak at $f_0$). In a **BRF**, the curve is a **valley shape** (dip at $f_0$). The X-axis represents frequency (log scale), and the Y-axis represents gain in dB.

## 4.4 Detailed Functional Architecture — Narrow-Band Notch Filter (Twin-T)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[Input Signal Vin] --> B[Twin-T Passive Network]
    B --> B1[Path 1: Resistor-Resistor-Capacitor T]
    B --> B2[Path 2: Capacitor-Capacitor-Resistor T]
    B1 --> C[OpAmp Non-Inverting Input]
    B2 --> D[OpAmp Inverting Input via Feedback]
    C --> E[Output Node Vout]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Notched Output: 50 Hz Removed]
    G[fn = 1 over 2piRC] -.-> B
    H[Q = 1 over 2 x 2 minus Av] -.-> E
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Functional Note:** The Twin-T topology achieves a **deep, narrow null** at $f_n$ by exploiting the phase opposition of the two T-paths. The op-amp provides gain $A_v$ that controls the **depth and Q** of the notch without loading the passive network.

### Question A1: Define Band Pass Filter. Mention its key parameters.

**[KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model]**

**Model Answer:**

A **Band Pass Filter (BPF)** is a frequency-selective circuit that allows signals within a specific range of frequencies (between a lower cutoff $f_L$ and an upper cutoff $f_H$) to pass through with minimum attenuation, while attenuating all frequencies outside this range.

**Key Parameters:**
1. **Lower Cutoff Frequency ($f_L$):** $\frac{1}{2\pi R_1 C_1}$ — set by the HPF stage.
2. **Upper Cutoff Frequency ($f_H$):** $\frac{1}{2\pi R_2 C_2}$ — set by the LPF stage.
3. **Bandwidth ($BW$):** $f_H - f_L$.
4. **Center Frequency ($f_0$):** $\sqrt{f_L \cdot f_H}$.
5. **Quality Factor ($Q$):** $\frac{f_0}{BW}$ — measure of selectivity.

---

### Question A2: What is a Notch Filter? Give one application.

**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Model]**

**Model Answer:**

A **Notch Filter** is a narrow-band band rejection filter that sharply attenuates a very specific frequency (called the **notch frequency** $f_n$) while passing all other frequencies with minimal loss. It has a very **high Q factor**.

**Notch Frequency:** $f_n = \dfrac{1}{2\pi RC}$

**Application:** Used in biomedical instrumentation (ECG/EEG amplifiers) to remove **50 Hz mains hum interference** without affecting the desired bio-signal frequencies (typically 0.5 Hz to 1 kHz).

### Question A (14 Marks) — Cascaded BPF Design

**[KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model | Module 2 | 14 Marks]**

**(a)** With the help of a neat block diagram, explain the realization of a **first-order Band Pass Filter** using a cascade of HPF and LPF stages. Derive the expressions for lower cutoff frequency, upper cutoff frequency, and bandwidth.

**(b)** A first-order BPF is realized by cascading an HPF ($R_1 = 4.7 \text{ k}\Omega$, $C_1 = 0.033 \text{ \mu F}$) and an LPF ($R_2 = 470 \text{ }\Omega$, $C_2 = 0.033 \text{ \mu F}$). Calculate:
   - (i) Lower cutoff frequency $f_L$
   - (ii) Upper cutoff frequency $f_H$
   - (iii) Center frequency $f_0$
   - (iv) Bandwidth $BW$
   - (v) Quality factor $Q$

#### Model Solution

**Part (a) — 7 Marks:**

A BPF is realized by **cascading a first-order HPF with a first-order LPF**, as shown in the block diagram below:

`[Input] → [HPF: R1, C1] → [Buffer] → [LPF: R2, C2] → [Output]`

**Derivation of $f_L$:** The HPF has the transfer function $H_{HPF}(s) = \frac{R_1 C_1 s}{1 + R_1 C_1 s}$. The cutoff ($-3$ dB) occurs when $\omega_L R_1 C_1 = 1$:

$$
f_L = \frac{1}{2\pi R_1 C_1}
$$

**Derivation of $f_H$:** The LPF has $H_{LPF}(s) = \frac{1}{1 + R_2 C_2 s}$. The cutoff occurs when $\omega_H R_2 C_2 = 1$:

$$
f_H = \frac{1}{2\pi R_2 C_2}
$$

**Derivation of Bandwidth:**

$$
BW = f_H - f_L = \frac{1}{2\pi R_2 C_2} - \frac{1}{2\pi R_1 C_1}
$$

**Center Frequency:**

$$
f_0 = \sqrt{f_L \cdot f_H}
$$

The HPF removes frequencies below $f_L$; the LPF removes frequencies above $f_H$. Only the band $f_L \leq f \leq f_H$ survives, giving a band pass response.

**Part (b) — 7 Marks:**

Given: $R_1 = 4.7 \text{ k}\Omega = 4.7 \times 10^3 \text{ }\Omega$, $C_1 = 0.033 \text{ \mu F} = 0.033 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}$, $R_2 = 470 \text{ }\Omega$, $C_2 = 0.033 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}$.

**(i) Lower cutoff frequency $f_L$:**

$$
f_L = \frac{1}{2\pi R_1 C_1} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 4.7 \times 10^3 \times 0.033 \times 10^{-6}}
$$

$$
f_L = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 1.551 \times 10^{-4}} = \frac{1}{9.745 \times 10^{-4}}
$$

$$
\boxed{f_L \approx 1026.2 \text{ Hz} \approx 1.026 \text{ kHz}}
$$

**(ii) Upper cutoff frequency $f_H$:**

$$
f_H = \frac{1}{2\pi R_2 C_2} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 470 \times 0.033 \times 10^{-6}}
$$

$$
f_H = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 1.551 \times 10^{-5}} = \frac{1}{9.745 \times 10^{-5}}
$$

$$
\boxed{f_H \approx 10262 \text{ Hz} \approx 10.26 \text{ kHz}}
$$

**(iii) Center frequency $f_0$:**

$$
f_0 = \sqrt{f_L \cdot f_H} = \sqrt{1026.2 \times 10262}
$$

$$
f_0 = \sqrt{1.053 \times 10^7} \approx 3245.4 \text{ Hz}
$$

$$
\boxed{f_0 \approx 3.245 \text{ kHz}}
$$

**(iv) Bandwidth $BW$:**

$$
BW = f_H - f_L = 10262 - 1026.2 = 9235.8 \text{ Hz}
$$

$$
\boxed{BW \approx 9.236 \text{ kHz}}
$$

**(v) Quality factor $Q$:**

$$
Q = \frac{f_0}{BW} = \frac{3245.4}{9235.8} \approx 0.351
$$

$$
\boxed{Q \approx 0.35}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **Examiner's Valuation Pitfall — Q for BPF:** Many students **incorrectly** write $Q = \dfrac{BW}{f_0}$ (reciprocal). This is the Q definition for an **RLC resonant circuit's bandwidth interpretation**, not the filter Q. The correct filter Q is $\dfrac{f_0}{BW}$. **Loses 1 mark** if reversed.

---

### Question B (14 Marks) — Band Rejection Filter Analysis

**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Model | Module 2 | 14 Marks]**

**(a)** With the help of a block diagram, explain the realization of a **wide-band Band Stop Filter** using parallel combination of LPF and HPF. Derive the transfer function.

**(b)** Design a Twin-T notch filter to reject **50 Hz mains hum** in a biomedical amplifier. Choose $R$ and $C$ appropriately. State the design equations used.

#### Model Solution

**Part (a) — 7 Marks:**

A **wide-band BSF** is realized using a **parallel combination** (summing) of an LPF and an HPF, both driven by the same input:

`[Input] → [Splitter] → [LPF] ─┐`
`              → [HPF] ─┴→ [Summing Amplifier] → [Output]`

The LPF passes low frequencies (below $f_H$); the HPF passes high frequencies (above $f_L$). In the band $f_L$ to $f_H$, neither path conducts strongly, creating a **stop band**.

**Transfer Function Derivation:**

$$
H_{BSF}(s) = H_{LPF}(s) + H_{HPF}(s)
$$

$$
H_{BSF}(s) = \frac{1}{1 + R_2 C_2 s} + \frac{R_1 C_1 s}{1 + R_1 C_1 s}
$$

Common denominator:

$$
H_{BSF}(s) = \frac{1 + R_1 C_1 s + R_1 C_1 s(1 + R_2 C_2 s)}{(1 + R_1 C_1 s)(1 + R_2 C_2 s)}
$$

$$
H_{BSF}(s) = \frac{1 + 2 R_1 C_1 s + R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2 s^2}{1 + (R_1 C_1 + R_2 C_2)s + R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2 s^2}
$$

**Verification:**
- At $s = 0$ (low freq): $H_{BSF} = 1$ → passes ✓
- At $s \to \infty$ (high freq): $H_{BSF} = 1$ → passes ✓
- In the middle: $|H_{BSF}| < 1$ → rejection ✓

**Part (b) — 7 Marks:**

**Design Specification:** Notch frequency $f_n = 50 \text{ Hz}$.

**Design Equation:**

$$
f_n = \frac{1}{2\pi RC} \quad \Rightarrow \quad RC = \frac{1}{2\pi f_n}
$$

**Step 1:** Compute RC product:

$$
RC = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 50} = \frac{1}{314.159} = 3.183 \times 10^{-3} \text{ seconds}
$$

**Step 2:** Choose a convenient value of $C$ and solve for $R$. Let $C = 0.1 \text{ \mu F} = 10^{-7} \text{ F}$:

$$
R = \frac{3.183 \times 10^{-3}}{10^{-7}} = 3.183 \times 10^4 \text{ }\Omega \approx 31.83 \text{ k}\Omega
$$

**Step 3:** Standardize component values:
- Choose $C = 0.1 \text{ \mu F}$ (standard)
- $R \approx 31.83 \text{ k}\Omega$ → use $33 \text{ k}\Omega$ (standard E12 value)

**Recalculated notch frequency with standard values:**

$$
f_n = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 33 \times 10^3 \times 0.1 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{2.0735 \times 10^{-2}}
$$

$$
f_n \approx 48.23 \text{ Hz}
$$

(Acceptable for 50 Hz notch — within ±5% tolerance.)

**Component Selection for Twin-T Network:**
- Two series resistors: $R = 33 \text{ k}\Omega$
- Shunt resistor: $R/2 = 16.5 \text{ k}\Omega \approx 16 \text{ k}\Omega$ (standard)
- Two series capacitors: $C = 0.1 \text{ \mu F}$
- Shunt capacitor: $2C = 0.2 \text{ \mu F}$

**Op-amp gain setting** for desired Q (say $Q = 5$):

$$
Q = \frac{1}{2(2 - A_v)} \quad \Rightarrow \quad 5 = \frac{1}{2(2 - A_v)}
$$

$$
2(2 - A_v) = \frac{1}{5} = 0.2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 2 - A_v = 0.1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad A_v = 1.9
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **Examiner's Valuation Pitfall — Notch Filter Component Ratios:** In a Twin-T network, the **shunt element** is **double** the series element ($2C$ and $R/2$). Students often write $C$ and $R$ for the shunt as well. This is the **most common mistake** in KTU exams on Twin-T filters. **Loses 2 marks** if the ratios are wrong.

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Pitfall & Warning Summary

> [!WARNING]
> **Top 5 Common Mistakes in KTU Module 2 Filter Questions:**
>
> 1. **Confusing $f_0$ formulas:** Writing $f_0 = (f_L + f_H)/2$ (arithmetic mean) instead of $\sqrt{f_L f_H}$ (geometric mean). **Penalty: 1 mark.**
>
> 2. **Inverted Q factor:** Writing $Q = BW/f_0$ instead of $Q = f_0/BW$. **Penalty: 1 mark.**
>
> 3. **BPF vs BSF confusion in cascade vs parallel:** Students often describe the BPF as parallel and BSF as cascade. Remember: **BPF = Cascade**, **BSF = Parallel/Sum**. **Penalty: 2–3 marks.**
>
> 4. **Missing units in final answer:** KTU valuators specifically check for units. Always write "Hz" or "kHz" after the numerical value. **Penalty: 0.5 mark per missing unit.**
>
> 5. **Forgetting to convert $\mu F$ to $F$ in RC product:** A common computation error leads to answers off by a factor of $10^6$. Always convert: $1 \text{ \mu F} = 10^{-6} \text{ F}$. **Penalty: full marks of the sub-part if answer is numerically wrong.**

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!TIP]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Module 2: Band Pass & Band Rejection Filters**

### A. Core Concepts (Must Know)

- A **Band Pass Filter (BPF)** passes frequencies between $f_L$ and $f_H$; rejects all others.
- A **Band Rejection Filter (BRF/BSF)** rejects frequencies between $f_L$ and $f_H$; passes all others.
- A **Notch Filter** is a narrow-band BRF with very high Q.
- BPF is realized by **cascading HPF + LPF** (series).
- BRF (wide-band) is realized by **summing LPF || HPF outputs** (parallel).
- Notch filter is realized using **Twin-T** or **Wien Bridge** topology.

### B. The 5 Key Formulas (Must Memorize)

1. $f_L = \dfrac{1}{2\pi R_1 C_1}$ — HPF stage
2. $f_H = \dfrac{1}{2\pi R_2 C_2}$ — LPF stage
3. $BW = f_H - f_L$
4. $f_0 = \sqrt{f_L \cdot f_H}$
5. $Q = \dfrac{f_0}{BW}$

### C. Design Rules of Thumb

- **Always** ensure $f_L < f_H$ (otherwise no pass band exists).
- **For symmetric BPF:** Choose $R_1 C_1 = R_2 C_2 = RC$ → $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi RC}$.
- **For high-Q narrow band:** $f_L$ and $f_H$ must be very close (e.g., 990 Hz and 1010 Hz → Q = 50).
- **Notch filter stability:** $A_v$ must be **strictly less than 2** to avoid oscillation.

### D. Applications (For 2-Mark Sub-Questions)

| Application | Filter | Why |
|---|---|---|
| AM Radio tuner | BPF | Select one station's carrier |
| ECG instrumentation | Notch (50/60 Hz) | Remove mains hum |
| Audio crossover | BPF/BRF | Direct frequencies to correct speakers |
| Spectrum analyzer | Variable BPF | Sweep and display |
| DSL line filters | BRF | Isolate voice from data bands |

### E. Common Units & Constants

- Frequency: **Hz** (or kHz, MHz for higher ranges)
- Capacitance: **Farads (F)** — always convert $\mu F$, nF, pF to F before calculation
- Resistance: **Ohms ($\Omega$)** — convert k$\Omega$ to $\Omega$
- Q factor: **dimensionless**
- Standard $\pi \approx 3.14159$, $2\pi \approx 6.28318$

### F. Exam Strategy (KTU 2024 ESE)

- For 14-mark questions, always draw the **block diagram first** (1 mark reserved).
- Show **every substitution** with proper units — partial marking is strict.
- Mention the **condition** $f_L < f_H$ explicitly in BPF/BRF derivations.
- For Notch filter, **state the Twin-T element ratios** ($R/2$ and $2C$) — this is the most-missed detail.

### G. Quick-Reference Mnemonic

> **"BPF = Cascade, BRF = Combine; Pass = Peak Hill, Stop = Notch Valley."**

> **"For filters, remember: $f_0$ is the **G**eometric mean, **N**ot arithmetic!"**

> **"Q is **Q**uotient: $f_0$ **Q**uotient over $BW$ — never reverse!"**

---

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PEEET411 - ELECTRONIC INSTRUMENTATION
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Pulse Amplitude Modulation

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Definition

**Pulse Amplitude Modulation (PAM)** is a pulse modulation technique in which the **amplitude of a periodic train of pulses** (the carrier) is varied in proportion to the **instantaneous amplitude** of the continuous-time message (baseband) signal, while the **pulse width and pulse position are held constant**.

Mathematically, the modulated signal is expressed as:

$$s(t) = m(t) \cdot p(t)$$

where $m(t)$ is the message signal and $p(t)$ is the rectangular pulse train.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight (Module 2):** PAM is treated as the **foundational pulse modulation scheme** from which all other pulse modulation techniques — PWM (Pulse Width Modulation), PPM (Pulse Position Modulation) and PCM (Pulse Code Modulation) — are conceptually derived. Every KTU question on pulse modulation begins from the PAM base.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Real-World Intuition

Imagine a **postage-stamp printing press**: the rotating drum (carrier) leaves a series of regular ink impressions on the paper. If you now raise or lower the **ink level of each impression** in step with the height of a sound wave, each stamp captures a *snapshot* of the sound wave at that instant. That, in essence, is PAM — a sequence of pulses whose **heights are stamped by the message waveform**.

- The **drum** → pulse carrier (regular spacing).
- The **ink level** → pulse amplitude.
- The **original sound wave** → message signal $m(t)$.

### 1.3 Standard Reference Metrics

| Metric | Symbol | Standard Value / Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Sampling Frequency | $f_s$ | $\geq 2 f_m$ (Hz) |
| Sampling Period | $T_s$ | $1 / f_s$ (seconds) |
| Pulse Width | $\tau$ | $\tau \ll T_s$ (seconds) |
| Duty Cycle | $D$ | $\tau / T_s$ (dimensionless) |
| Maximum Message Frequency | $f_m$ | Hz |

> [!NOTE]
> **Why "$\tau \ll T_s$"?** Narrow pulses mean that the signal occupies only a small fraction of each sampling period. This preserves the **spectral gap** between replicas of $M(f)$, allowing a low-pass filter at the receiver to reconstruct $m(t)$ cleanly. This concept is heavily tested in KTU derivations.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The Two Principal Variants of PAM

#### (a) Natural-Sampled PAM (Natural PAM)
The **pulse tops follow the shape of $m(t)$** during the pulse duration. Achieved by passing $m(t)$ through a **gates / chopper / sampling switch** that is closed only during the pulse width $\tau$.

#### (b) Flat-Top PAM (Sample-and-Hold PAM)
The **pulse tops are flat**, with amplitude equal to the value of $m(t)$ at the **sampling instant**. Implemented using a **sample-and-hold (S/H) circuit** or a **zero-order hold**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Why two variants?** Natural PAM preserves $m(t)$'s shape, but is **hard to regenerate** because noise distorts the pulse tops. Flat-top PAM is **easy to generate, regenerate, and decode** (especially for TDM), but introduces an aperture-effect distortion $\text{sinc}(f\tau)$ that must be compensated.

### 2.2 Operational Logic — Generation (Bullet Steps)

1. The message signal $m(t)$ is fed to one input of an **analog multiplier / chopper**.
2. A **pulse train generator** produces $p(t)$, a periodic sequence of rectangular pulses of width $\tau$ and period $T_s$.
3. The **multiplier output** is $s(t) = m(t) \cdot p(t)$.
4. For **flat-top PAM**, the multiplier is followed by a **sample-and-hold amplifier** that locks the amplitude to $m(nT_s)$ until the next sample.
5. The output spectrum $S(f)$ contains replicas of $M(f)$ centred at $k f_s$.

### 2.3 Operational Logic — Demoduction (Reception)

1. The received PAM waveform $s(t)$ is applied to a **low-pass filter (LPF)**.
2. The LPF has cutoff frequency $f_c$ such that $f_m < f_c < (f_s - f_m)$.
3. The LPF passes the **baseband replica** centred at $k = 0$ and rejects all higher spectral replicas.
4. For flat-top PAM, an **equalization filter** of gain $1 / \text{sinc}(f\tau)$ compensates for the aperture effect.

### 2.4 The "Why" Behind Each Step

- **Multiplication in time** ↔ **Convolution in frequency** — this is the spectral duplication principle.
- **LPF cutoff placement** — avoids **aliasing** while preserving the original message spectrum.
- **Equalization** — restores the high-frequency content attenuated by the flat-top shape.

### 2.5 KTU Formula Sheet (High-Yield Cheat Sheet)

| Quantity | Expression | Notes / Units |
|---|---|---|
| Pulse Train (Fourier Series) | $p(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k \, e^{j 2 \pi k f_s t}$ | $f_s = 1/T_s$ |
| Fourier Coefficient | $C_k = (A \tau / T_s) \, \text{sinc}(k f_s \tau)$ | $A$ = pulse amplitude |
| Natural PAM Time-Domain | $s(t) = m(t) \cdot p(t)$ | Continuous time |
| Flat-Top PAM Time-Domain | $s(t) = \sum_{n} m(nT_s) \, h(t - nT_s)$ | $h(t)$ = rect pulse |
| Natural PAM Spectrum | $S(f) = (A\tau/T_s) \sum_{k} M(f - k f_s)$ | Ideal scaling |
| Flat-Top PAM Spectrum | $S(f) = (A\tau/T_s) \, \text{sinc}(f\tau) \, e^{-j\pi f \tau} \sum_{k} M(f - k f_s)$ | Aperture effect present |
| Sinc Function | $\text{sinc}(x) = \sin(\pi x) / (\pi x)$ | Note: KTU uses normalised sinc |
| Nyquist Rate | $f_s \geq 2 f_m$ | Hz |
| Duty Cycle | $D = \tau / T_s$ | Dimensionless, $0 < D < 1$ |
| Reconstruction Filter Cutoff | $f_m < f_c < f_s - f_m$ | Hz |
| Aperture Effect Equalizer | $H_{eq}(f) = 1 / [\text{sinc}(f\tau) \, e^{-j\pi f\tau}]$ | Compensates flat-top droop |
| Transmission Bandwidth | $BW \approx f_s$ (theoretical), $\approx 1/\tau$ (practical) | Hz |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Critical KTU Pitfall:** Many textbooks define $\text{sinc}(x) = \sin(x)/x$ (unnormalised). KTU 2024 papers follow the **normalized** $\text{sinc}(x) = \sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$. Always check which convention your derivation uses. This is a frequent 1-mark loss in valuation.

### 2.6 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Building block** for Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) — multiple PAM signals time-share one channel.
- **Front-end** for PCM — natural/flat-top PAM is the **first stage** before quantization and encoding.
- **Industrial telemetry** — slowly varying physical quantities (temperature, pressure) are transmitted as PAM over long wires.
- **Biological signal acquisition** — ECG, EEG instruments use sample-and-hold PAM for digital recording.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation 1 — Fourier Series of the Pulse Train $p(t)$

**Statement:** Express a periodic rectangular pulse train of amplitude $A$, width $\tau$ and period $T_s$ as a Fourier series.

**Step 1 — Define one pulse.** A single rectangular pulse of width $\tau$ centred at the origin:

$$h(t) = \begin{cases} A, & \vert t \vert \leq \tau/2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

**Step 2 — Periodise.** The pulse train is:

$$p(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} h(t - nT_s)$$

**Step 3 — Compute Fourier coefficient.**

$$C_k = \frac{1}{T_s} \int_{-T_s/2}^{T_s/2} p(t) \, e^{-j 2\pi k f_s t} \, dt$$

**Step 4 — Because only the pulse at $n = 0$ lies within one period:**

$$C_k = \frac{1}{T_s} \int_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2} A \, e^{-j 2\pi k f_s t} \, dt$$

**Step 5 — Perform integration.**

$$C_k = \frac{A}{T_s} \left[ \frac{e^{-j 2\pi k f_s t}}{-j 2\pi k f_s} \right]_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}$$

$$C_k = \frac{A}{T_s} \cdot \frac{e^{-j \pi k f_s \tau} - e^{j \pi k f_s \tau}}{-j 2\pi k f_s}$$

**Step 6 — Use Euler's identity** $\sin(x) = (e^{jx} - e^{-jx})/(2j)$:

$$C_k = \frac{A}{T_s} \cdot \frac{2 \sin(\pi k f_s \tau)}{2\pi k f_s}$$

$$\boxed{C_k = \frac{A\tau}{T_s} \, \text{sinc}(k f_s \tau)}$$

where $\text{sinc}(x) = \sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$.

---

### 3.2 Derivation 2 — Spectrum of Natural-Sampled PAM

**Statement:** Obtain the spectrum $S(f)$ of $s(t) = m(t) \cdot p(t)$.

**Step 1 — Fourier series expansion of $p(t)$:**

$$p(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k \, e^{j 2\pi k f_s t}$$

**Step 2 — Multiply by $m(t)$:**

$$s(t) = m(t) \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k \, e^{j 2\pi k f_s t}$$

**Step 3 — Apply frequency-shift property** $\mathcal{F}\{m(t) e^{j 2\pi k f_s t}\} = M(f - k f_s)$:

$$S(f) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k \, M(f - k f_s)$$

**Step 4 — Substitute $C_k$ from Derivation 1:**

$$\boxed{S(f) = \frac{A\tau}{T_s} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \text{sinc}(k f_s \tau) \, M(f - k f_s)}$$

**Step 5 — Physical interpretation:**

- The baseband ($k = 0$) replica $M(f)$ is scaled by $A\tau/T_s$ (the average DC value of $p(t)$).
- Higher-order replicas ($k \neq 0$) are **attenuated** by $\text{sinc}(k f_s \tau)$.
- For $\tau \ll T_s$, $\text{sinc}(k f_s \tau) \to 1$ and **all replicas carry equal weight**.

---

### 3.3 Derivation 3 — Spectrum of Flat-Top PAM

**Statement:** Derive the spectrum of flat-top PAM generated via zero-order hold.

**Step 1 — Time-domain expression.** Each sample $m(nT_s)$ is held for $\tau$ seconds:

$$s(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} m(nT_s) \, h(t - nT_s)$$

where $h(t) = \text{rect}(t/\tau)$ is the rectangular hold pulse.

**Step 2 — Equivalent representation.** Let $m_s(t) = \sum_n m(nT_s) \, \delta(t - nT_s)$ be the **impulse-sampled** message. Then:

$$s(t) = m_s(t) * h(t)$$

**Step 3 — Spectrum.** Convolution in time $\Leftrightarrow$ multiplication in frequency:

$$S(f) = M_s(f) \cdot H(f)$$

**Step 4 — Spectrum of impulse-sampled signal** (sampling theorem):

$$M_s(f) = f_s \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} M(f - k f_s)$$

**Step 5 — Spectrum of rectangular hold pulse:**

$$H(f) = \tau \, \text{sinc}(f\tau) \, e^{-j\pi f \tau}$$

**Step 6 — Combine (Steps 3, 4, 5):**

$$S(f) = f_s \, \tau \, \text{sinc}(f\tau) \, e^{-j\pi f \tau} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} M(f - k f_s)$$

$$\boxed{S(f) = \frac{\tau}{T_s} \, \text{sinc}(f\tau) \, e^{-j\pi f \tau} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} M(f - k f_s)}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Difference Between Natural and Flat-Top:**
> - Natural PAM: $\text{sinc}$ attenuation depends on **spectral index** $k$ only (carrier-related).
> - Flat-Top PAM: $\text{sinc}$ attenuation depends on **frequency** $f$ continuously (aperture effect).
> - The exponential $e^{-j\pi f \tau}$ introduces a **linear phase delay** of $\tau/2$.

---

### 3.4 Reconstruction (Demodulation) Logic

After transmission through an ideal channel:

**Step 1 — Apply LPF** with cutoff $f_c$ where $f_m < f_c < f_s - f_m$.

**Step 2 — For natural PAM, output is:**

$$m_{rec}(t) = \frac{A\tau}{T_s} \, m(t)$$

A simple gain stage recovers $m(t)$.

**Step 3 — For flat-top PAM, output is distorted:**

$$M_{rec}(f) = \frac{\tau}{T_s} \, \text{sinc}(f\tau) \, e^{-j\pi f \tau} \, M(f)$$

**Step 4 — Cascade an equalizer** $H_{eq}(f) = \dfrac{1}{\text{sinc}(f\tau)} \, e^{j\pi f \tau}$ to compensate:

$$M_{eq}(f) = \frac{\tau}{T_s} \, M(f)$$

Hence $m_{eq}(t) = (\tau/T_s) \, m(t)$ — exact recovery.

---

### 3.5 Worked Numerical Example (KTU-Style)

**Problem:** A 4 kHz sinusoid $m(t) = 5 \cos(2\pi \cdot 4000 \, t)$ is sampled by natural PAM using pulses of amplitude $A = 10$ V, width $\tau = 25 \, \mu$s, and sampling frequency $f_s = 20$ kHz. Find the spectrum amplitude of the baseband replica.

**Solution:**

$$\text{Scale factor} = \frac{A\tau}{T_s} = \frac{10 \cdot 25 \times 10^{-6}}{50 \times 10^{-6}} = 5$$

Since $M(f)$ for a cosine has two impulses of strength $2.5$ each at $\pm 4$ kHz:

$$S(f) = 5 \cdot \sum_k \text{sinc}(k f_s \tau) \, M(f - k f_s)$$

Baseband replica ($k = 0$) has total amplitude scaling $\times 5$.

For $k = 1$: $f_s \tau = 20{,}000 \times 25 \times 10^{-6} = 0.5 \Rightarrow \text{sinc}(0.5) = 2/\pi \approx 0.637$. So the first replica is attenuated to $63.7\%$ of its true amplitude.

> [!NOTE]
> This attenuation of side-band replicas is precisely why PAM (without further coding) is **bandwidth-inefficient**. KTU PCM questions reference this fact to justify the move to PCM.
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

### Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

#### Q1. `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]`
**Define Pulse Amplitude Modulation. Distinguish between Natural PAM and Flat-Top PAM.**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**

PAM is a pulse modulation scheme in which the **amplitude of each pulse in a periodic train** is varied in proportion to the instantaneous value of the message signal $m(t)$, while **pulse width and pulse position remain constant**.

| Feature | Natural PAM | Flat-Top PAM |
|---|---|---|
| Pulse Top Shape | Follows $m(t)$ during $\tau$ | Flat (held at $m(nT_s)$) |
| Generation | Chopper / analog gate | Sample-and-hold (S/H) |
| Spectral Sinc Attenuation | On $k$ only | On $f$ continuously |
| Ease of Regeneration | Difficult | Easy (used in TDM/PCM) |
| Demodulation | Simple LPF | LPF + equalizer |

**(1 mark)** definition, **(1 mark)** each distinction row = full 3 marks.

---

#### Q2. `[KTU University Exam – Jun 2024]`
**State the Nyquist criterion for sampling. Why is $f_s > 2 f_m$ preferred over $f_s = 2 f_m$ in practical PAM systems?**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**

**Nyquist Criterion:** A bandlimited message signal of maximum frequency $f_m$ can be uniquely reconstructed from its samples **iff** $f_s \geq 2 f_m$.

Although $f_s = 2 f_m$ is theoretically sufficient, in practice $f_s > 2 f_m$ is preferred because:

1. **(1 mark)** A practical low-pass filter cannot have an infinitely sharp cutoff; it requires a **transition band** between $f_m$ and $(f_s - f_m)$.
2. **(1 mark)** Guard band prevents **aliasing** caused by slight drifts in $f_s$ or $f_m$.
3. **(1 mark)** Allows margin for clock jitter and channel-induced phase distortion.

---

### Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

#### QUESTION A (14 Marks) `[KTU University Exam – Model Paper, Module 2]`

**(a)** Derive the expression for the **spectrum of natural-sampled PAM signal**. Clearly show the spectral replicas and explain how the original message signal can be recovered. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** A message signal $m(t)$ has bandwidth $f_m = 5$ kHz. It is sampled by natural PAM using pulses of amplitude $A = 8$ V, pulse width $\tau = 20 \, \mu$s and sampling frequency $f_s = 20$ kHz.
  - **(i)** Verify whether the Nyquist criterion is satisfied.
  - **(ii)** Calculate the duty cycle.
  - **(iii)** Determine the amplitude scaling factor of the baseband replica.
  - **(iv)** Find the attenuation factor of the first spectral replica. **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Derivation (7 marks)**

Step 1: Express $p(t)$ as Fourier series **(1 mark)**

$$p(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k \, e^{j 2\pi k f_s t}, \quad C_k = \frac{A\tau}{T_s} \, \text{sinc}(k f_s \tau)$$

Step 2: Multiply by $m(t)$ **(1 mark)**

$$s(t) = m(t) \cdot p(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k \, m(t) \, e^{j 2\pi k f_s t}$$

Step 3: Take Fourier transform using frequency-shift property **(2 marks)**

$$S(f) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k \, M(f - k f_s)$$

Step 4: Substitute $C_k$ **(1 mark)**

$$S(f) = \frac{A\tau}{T_s} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \text{sinc}(k f_s \tau) \, M(f - k f_s)$$

Step 5: Recovery **(2 marks)** — Pass $s(t)$ through an LPF of cutoff $f_m < f_c < f_s - f_m$. The baseband replica passes; all $k \neq 0$ replicas are rejected. Output is $(A\tau/T_s) \, m(t)$, which is the original message scaled.

**(b) Numerical (7 marks)**

**(i)** Nyquist check **(1 mark)**:

$$f_s = 20 \text{ kHz} \geq 2 f_m = 10 \text{ kHz} \quad \checkmark$$

**(ii)** Duty cycle **(2 marks)**:

$$T_s = 1/f_s = 50 \, \mu\text{s}, \quad D = \tau / T_s = 20/50 = 0.4 = 40\%$$

**(iii)** Baseband scaling **(2 marks)**:

$$\text{Scale} = \frac{A\tau}{T_s} = \frac{8 \times 20 \times 10^{-6}}{50 \times 10^{-6}} = 3.2$$

**(iv)** Attenuation of first replica ($k = 1$) **(2 marks)**:

$$k f_s \tau = 1 \times 20{,}000 \times 20 \times 10^{-6} = 0.4$$

$$\text{sinc}(0.4) = \sin(0.4\pi) / (0.4\pi) = \sin(72^\circ)/1.2566 \approx 0.9355 / 1.2566 \approx 0.7572$$

Attenuation ≈ **75.72 %**.

---

#### QUESTION B (14 Marks — Alternative Choice) `[KTU University Exam – Model Paper, Module 2]`

**(a)** Explain the **generation and detection of Flat-Top PAM** with neat block diagrams. Derive its spectrum. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Compare **Natural and Flat-Top PAM** in terms of (i) generation complexity, (ii) immunity to noise, (iii) ease of regeneration for TDM, (iv) spectral efficiency. State **two applications** of PAM. **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Generation, Detection, Spectrum of Flat-Top PAM (7 marks)**

**Generation (2 marks):** A sample-and-hold (S/H) circuit, clocked at $f_s$, samples $m(t)$ at $t = nT_s$ and holds the value for $\tau$ seconds via a capacitor. Output:

$$s(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} m(nT_s) \, \text{rect}\!\left(\frac{t - nT_s - \tau/2}{\tau}\right)$$

**Detection (2 marks):** LPF with cutoff $f_c$ where $f_m < f_c < f_s - f_m$, followed by an equalizer $H_{eq}(f) = 1/[\text{sinc}(f\tau) e^{-j\pi f\tau}]$ to compensate aperture droop.

**Spectrum (3 marks):**

$$S(f) = \frac{\tau}{T_s} \, \text{sinc}(f\tau) \, e^{-j\pi f\tau} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} M(f - k f_s)$$

- The exponential $e^{-j\pi f\tau}$ represents **constant time delay** of $\tau/2$.
- The factor $\text{sinc}(f\tau)$ represents the **aperture effect** (high-frequency roll-off).

**(b) Comparison (7 marks — distribute 1.5 marks each + 1 mark for applications)**

| Parameter | Natural PAM | Flat-Top PAM |
|---|---|---|
| Generation Complexity | Simple chopper | Requires S/H circuit |
| Noise Immunity | Low (pulse top carries noise) | Better (flat top can be regenerated) |
| Regeneration for TDM | Difficult | Easy (held value is stable) |
| Spectral Efficiency | Replicas attenuated by sinc($k f_s \tau$) | Continuous sinc($f\tau$) droop |
| Equalization Needed | No | Yes (aperture equalizer) |

**Applications (1 mark):** (i) Front-end for PCM, (ii) Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM), (iii) Industrial telemetry, (iv) Biological signal sampling.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Mark-Loss Traps:**
> 1. **Confusing sinc conventions** — $\sin(x)/x$ vs $\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$ can flip signs and numerics; KTU uses normalised sinc.
> 2. **Forgetting the exponential phase term** $e^{-j\pi f\tau}$ in flat-top derivation loses 1 mark.
> 3. **Wrong duty-cycle units** — always express as a fraction (0–1) AND percentage.
> 4. **Skipping the Nyquist check** in numericals — losing 1 easy mark.
> 5. **Equalizer missing** for flat-top PAM reconstruction — a frequent 1-mark deduction.

---

### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist)

- **PAM** varies **pulse amplitude** according to message; pulse width and position are **fixed**.
- **Two variants:** Natural (pulse top = message) and Flat-Top (pulse top held constant).
- **Nyquist rate:** $f_s \geq 2 f_m$ — strict theoretical minimum.
- **Duty cycle:** $D = \tau / T_s$; narrow pulses ($D \ll 1$) preserve spectral separation.
- **Natural PAM spectrum:** $S(f) = (A\tau/T_s) \sum_k \text{sinc}(k f_s \tau) \, M(f - k f_s)$.
- **Flat-Top PAM spectrum:** includes $\text{sinc}(f\tau) \, e^{-j\pi f\tau}$ — the **aperture effect**.
- **Demodulation:** LPF with cutoff $f_m < f_c < f_s - f_m$.
- **Equalizer** needed for flat-top PAM to undo $\text{sinc}(f\tau)$ droop.
- **PAM is the foundation** of PWM, PPM and PCM — KTU tests this hierarchy.
- **Applications:** PCM front-end, TDM, telemetry, biomedical signal acquisition.
- **KTU High-Yield Trick:** Side-replicas are attenuated by $\text{sinc}(k f_s \tau)$; for $k f_s \tau < 0.5$, attenuation is mild — choose $\tau$ carefully to avoid spectral overlap (aliasing).
- **Sinc convention:** Normalised $\text{sinc}(x) = \sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$ — used throughout KTU 2024 papers.
- **Phase term** $e^{-j\pi f\tau}$ in flat-top PAM = **constant group delay** of $\tau/2$ seconds.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PEEET411 - ELECTRONIC INSTRUMENTATION
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Profibus

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# SECTION 1 — Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **PROFIBUS (Process Field Bus)** is a standardized, open, vendor-independent fieldbus communication protocol defined under the international standards **IEC 61158** and **IEC 61784**, widely used in industrial automation for real-time distributed control of sensors, actuators, and controllers.

PROFIBUS is a serial bit-serial fieldbus system that links field devices (transmitters, valves, drives, motor starters, analyzers) to a central controller (PLC / DCS) using a single twisted-pair cable or fiber-optic medium. It is governed by the **PROFIBUS International (PI)** organization, and it is the most widely installed fieldbus worldwide, with over **50 million** devices in operation globally.

The PROFIBUS family is officially divided into three major protocol variants, each optimized for a specific class of industrial application:

| Variant | Full Form | Primary Application | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PROFIBUS-DP** | Decentralized Periphery | Factory automation, fast I/O | 9.6 kbps – 12 Mbps |
| **PROFIBUS-PA** | Process Automation | Hazardous area process control | **31.25 kbps** (fixed) |
| **PROFIBUS-FMS** | Fieldbus Message Specification | Controller-to-controller (legacy) | Up to 1.5 Mbps |

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The Industrial Postal System

> [!NOTE]
> **Intuition:** Think of a large factory as a busy city, and PROFIBUS as the **single two-lane highway** that connects every building (field device) to the city hall (the master PLC).

- **Master devices** are like the **postal department headquarters** — they hold the *token* (the right to speak).
- **Slave devices** (sensors, valves) are like **letter boxes** — they can only talk when the postman (master) hands them a request.
- The **token** is the only "speaking permit" on the bus. Whichever master holds the token gets exclusive rights to ask any slave a question or send a command for a small slice of time.
- The **twisted pair cable** is the highway. Even if it's broken or shorted at one point, **terminating resistors** at the ends of the highway prevent signal reflections, ensuring clean data.

This analogy captures the master-slave + token-passing nature of PROFIBUS in a way a beginner will never forget.

## 1.3 KTU Syllabus Highlights

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Board-Favorite Takeaways for Module 2:**
> 1. PROFIBUS protocol stack (OSI layers)
> 2. **PROFIBUS-DP, PROFIBUS-PA, PROFIBUS-FMS** — three variants
> 3. **RS-485 physical layer** characteristics
> 4. **Token passing** bus access method
> 5. **Telegram / frame structure** of PROFIBUS-DP
> 6. Comparison with other fieldbuses (Foundation Fieldbus, HART, Modbus)
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2 — Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 PROFIBUS Protocol Architecture (OSI Model Mapping)

PROFIBUS implements a **streamlined version of the OSI 7-layer model**, focusing only on the layers that are essential for industrial communication. This is a deliberate design choice to minimize overhead and maximize speed.

| OSI Layer | PROFIBUS Implementation | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Layer 7 — Application | **FMS / DP / PA Services** | Read/write process variables, diagnostics |
| Layer 6 — Presentation | Not used | — |
| Layer 5 — Session | Not used | — |
| Layer 4 — Transport | Not used | — |
| Layer 3 — Network | Not used | — |
| Layer 2 — Data Link | **FDL (Fieldbus Data Link)** | Bus access (token + polling), framing, error detection |
| Layer 1 — Physical | **RS-485 / Fiber / IEC 61158-2** | Electrical/optical signal transmission |

> [!NOTE]
> **Exam Tip:** The reason PROFIBUS skips layers 3-6 is that in a single-bus factory network, routing (Layer 3) is unnecessary — every device is on the same cable. This simplification gives PROFIBUS its trademark **deterministic, real-time performance**.

## 2.2 The Three PROFIBUS Variants — Detailed Comparison

### (a) PROFIBUS-DP (Decentralized Periphery) — The Workhorse
- **Designed for:** High-speed communication between a controller (master) and distributed I/O (slaves).
- **Speed:** 9.6 kbps up to **12 Mbps**.
- **Topology:** Line (bus) with terminating resistors (220 Ω) at both ends.
- **Cable:** Shielded twisted pair (Type A — purple sheath, recommended).
- **Max nodes per segment:** 32 (up to 126 with 4 repeaters).
- **Max segment length:** Depends on baud rate (see formula sheet).
- **Service modes:** DP-V0 (cyclic I/O), DP-V1 (acyclic read/write + alarms), DP-V2 (isochronous mode for motion control).

### (b) PROFIBUS-PA (Process Automation) — The Hazardous-Area Specialist
- **Designed for:** Process industries (chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical) — particularly **explosive atmospheres**.
- **Speed:** Fixed at **31.25 kbps**.
- **Physical layer:** **IEC 61158-2** — Manchester-coded, two-wire, **bus-powered** (devices draw power from the same cable).
- **Intrinsic safety (IS):** The current is limited to <100 mA, allowing safe operation in **Ex zones** (Zone 0/1).
- **Connection to DP:** Always used in conjunction with a **DP/PA coupler** or **PA link** that bridges to the high-speed DP backbone.

### (c) PROFIBUS-FMS (Fieldbus Message Specification) — The Legacy Communicator
- **Designed for:** Communication between controllers (peer-to-peer) at moderate speed.
- **Status:** **Largely obsolete** — replaced by Industrial Ethernet (PROFINET).
- **Service:** Rich set of broadcast and multicast services for object dictionaries.

## 2.3 Bus Access Method — Token Passing + Master-Slave Polling

PROFIBUS uses a **hybrid access method**, which is the heart of its determinism:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Two-Tier Access Strategy of PROFIBUS:**
> 1. **Among Masters (Token Ring):** Active masters (Class 1) form a logical token ring. The token is a special 3-byte telegram that circulates from one master to the next in a defined order. Only the master currently holding the token may initiate communication.
> 2. **Master to Slaves (Polling):** When a master holds the token, it either polls its assigned slaves (request-response) or broadcasts a command to all slaves.

This dual mechanism guarantees that **no two masters ever transmit simultaneously**, eliminating the bus contention that plagues Ethernet (until CSMA/CD resolves it). The result is a **bounded worst-case latency** — critical for real-time control loops.

## 2.4 Physical Layer — RS-485 Characteristics

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Topology | Linear bus, terminated at both ends |
| Cable | Shielded twisted pair, 2-wire |
| Termination | 220 Ω at each end (matches ~150 Ω cable impedance) |
| Voltage levels | Differential: ≥ ±1.5 V (logic), ≤ ±200 mV (idle) |
| Max stations per segment | 32 (with 9.6 kbps, up to 126 with repeaters) |
| Maximum distance | Baud-rate dependent (see table below) |
| Connector | D-sub 9-pin, M12, or terminal block |

## 2.5 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The following formulas are high-yield for KTU numericals — memorize them.**

### 2.5.1 Byte-to-Bit Conversion (UART Framing)

Each data byte in PROFIBUS uses **11 bits** (1 start + 8 data + 1 even parity + 1 stop):

$$N_{bits} = 11 \times N_{bytes}$$

### 2.5.2 Telegram Transmission Time

$$T_{tx} = \frac{11 \times (L_{header} + L_{data})}{B}$$

where:
- $B$ = Baud rate in bits per second
- $L_{header}$ = 11 bytes (fixed overhead for SD, LE, LEr, DA, SA, FC, FCS, ED, etc.)
- $L_{data}$ = user data length (1 to 244 bytes for DP-V0)

### 2.5.3 Maximum Segment Length vs Baud Rate (RS-485)

$$L_{max} \propto \frac{1}{B}$$

| Baud Rate $B$ (kbps) | Max Segment Length $L_{max}$ (m) |
|---|---|
| 9.6 | 1200 |
| 19.2 | 1200 |
| 93.75 | 1200 |
| 187.5 | 1000 |
| 500 | 400 |
| 1500 | 200 |
| 3000 | 100 |
| 6000 | 100 |
| **12000** | **100** |

### 2.5.4 Bus Cycle Time (Multi-Master System)

The total bus cycle time for a PROFIBUS network is given by:

$$T_{cycle} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} T_{TR,i} + T_{idle}$$

where:
- $m$ = number of active masters
- $T_{TR,i}$ = Token Rotation Time for master $i$
- $T_{idle}$ = idle gap between token rotations

The **Target Token Rotation Time** ($T_{TTR}$) is a configurable parameter that bounds the worst-case waiting time a master experiences before regaining the token.

### 2.5.5 Maximum Number of Stations

$$N_{stations} = 32 \times (1 + R)$$

where $R$ = number of repeaters (each repeater isolates and regenerates a new segment, max $R = 4$, so max $N_{stations} = 160$ — practically 126 since address range is 0–127 with 0 reserved and 127 for broadcast).

### 2.5.6 PROFIBUS-PA Current & Power Budget

The PA segment must provide sufficient current to all field devices:

$$I_{bus} \geq \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{device,j} + I_{fault} \leq 100 \text{ mA (IS limit)}$$

where:
- $I_{device,j}$ = basic current of device $j$ (typically 10–17 mA)
- $I_{fault}$ = additional current for FDE (Fault Disconnect Electronics) — typically 9 mA

## 2.6 Real-World Engineering Utility

PROFIBUS is the **silent nervous system** of modern industry. It is the dominant bus in:
- **Automotive manufacturing** (BMW, Mercedes, Volkswagen plants)
- **Chemical & petrochemical plants** (via PROFIBUS-PA with IS protection)
- **Water and wastewater treatment** plants
- **Power plants and steel mills**
- **Discrete manufacturing** (PROFIBUS-DP for conveyor, drives, robots)

Its deterministic behavior — a slave can be polled within a known, bounded time — is what makes motion control and closed-loop process control possible over a single cable.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# SECTION 3 — Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Exhaustive Derivation 1 — Telegram Transmission Time

**Problem Statement:** A PROFIBUS-DP master sends a request telegram with **6 bytes of user data** to a slave at a baud rate of **1.5 Mbps**. The slave returns a response with **10 bytes of user data**. Calculate the total request-response time, ignoring propagation delay and slave processing time.

### Step 1: Identify the Header Length

For PROFIBUS-DP, the fixed telegram header (and trailer) consists of:
- SD (Start Delimiter): 1 byte
- LE (Length): 1 byte
- LEr (Length repeated): 1 byte
- DA (Destination Address): 1 byte
- SA (Source Address): 1 byte
- FC (Function Code): 1 byte
- FCS (Frame Check Sequence): 1 byte
- ED (End Delimiter): 1 byte

**Total header bytes** $L_{header} = 8$ bytes (depending on variant — DP-V0/DP-V1 typically use 11 bytes including protocol overhead; we will use the commonly-quoted **11-byte overhead** for safety in KTU exam answers).

> [!NOTE]
> For an exam-safe answer, always state: $L_{header} = 11$ bytes (including protocol control bytes such as PDU and padding).

### Step 2: Request Transmission Time

$$T_{req} = \frac{11 \times (L_{header} + L_{data,req})}{B}$$

Substituting $L_{header} = 11$ bytes, $L_{data,req} = 6$ bytes, $B = 1.5 \times 10^6$ bps:

$$T_{req} = \frac{11 \times (11 + 6)}{1.5 \times 10^6}$$

$$T_{req} = \frac{11 \times 17}{1.5 \times 10^6} = \frac{187}{1.5 \times 10^6}$$

$$T_{req} = 1.2467 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s} = 124.67 \text{ μs}$$

### Step 3: Response Transmission Time

$$T_{res} = \frac{11 \times (L_{header} + L_{data,res})}{B}$$

Substituting $L_{data,res} = 10$ bytes:

$$T_{res} = \frac{11 \times (11 + 10)}{1.5 \times 10^6} = \frac{11 \times 21}{1.5 \times 10^6}$$

$$T_{res} = \frac{231}{1.5 \times 10^6} = 1.54 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s} = 154 \text{ μs}$$

### Step 4: Total Request-Response Time

$$T_{total} = T_{req} + T_{res}$$

$$T_{total} = 124.67 \text{ μs} + 154 \text{ μs} = 278.67 \text{ μs}$$

### Step 5: Interpretation

> The total transaction is completed in **less than 300 μs** — fast enough to scan **3,500 slaves per second** theoretically. This is why PROFIBUS-DP at 1.5 Mbps is the preferred choice for high-speed packaging lines and motion control.

---

## 3.2 Exhaustive Derivation 2 — Maximum Number of Slaves per Network

**Problem Statement:** A PROFIBUS-DP network is built using **3 repeaters**. Each segment has the standard 32-station capacity. What is the maximum number of slaves (excluding masters) that can be addressed? Address 0 is reserved for the service unit, and address 127 is used for broadcast.

### Step 1: Total Station Capacity

$$N_{stations} = 32 \times (1 + R)$$

Substituting $R = 3$:

$$N_{stations} = 32 \times (1 + 3) = 32 \times 4 = 128$$

### Step 2: Subtract Reserved Addresses

The total address space is 0–127 (128 addresses). Subtract:
- Address 0 → service/master service unit
- Address 127 → broadcast

$$N_{usable} = 128 - 2 = 126$$

### Step 3: Subtract Master Addresses

Assuming **2 active masters (Class 1)** are present:

$$N_{slaves,max} = 126 - 2 = 124$$

### Step 4: Final Answer

> The network can address up to **124 slave devices** plus 2 active masters, 1 service master, and a broadcast address, for a total of 126 usable stations across 4 segments.

---

## 3.3 Exhaustive Derivation 3 — Token Rotation Time in a Multi-Master System

**Problem Statement:** A PROFIBUS network has **3 Class 1 masters** (M1, M2, M3). The target token rotation time is set to $T_{TTR} = 10$ ms. Each master polls on average **20 slaves** with **4 bytes of data per transaction** at **500 kbps**. Header overhead is 11 bytes. Compute the **approximate bus cycle time** and check whether it is within the deterministic bound.

### Step 1: Transmission Time per Transaction

$$T_{tx} = \frac{11 \times (11 + 4)}{500 \times 10^3} = \frac{11 \times 15}{5 \times 10^5} = \frac{165}{5 \times 10^5} = 3.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s} = 330 \text{ μs}$$

### Step 2: Time per Master (20 slaves polled)

$$T_{master} = 20 \times T_{tx} = 20 \times 330 \text{ μs} = 6600 \text{ μs} = 6.6 \text{ ms}$$

### Step 3: Total Token Rotation Time

$$T_{TR,total} = \sum_{i=1}^{3} T_{master,i} = 3 \times 6.6 \text{ ms} = 19.8 \text{ ms}$$

### Step 4: Compare with $T_{TTR}$

$$T_{TR,total} = 19.8 \text{ ms} > T_{TTR} = 10 \text{ ms}$$

### Step 5: Conclusion

> The actual token rotation time **exceeds** the configured target. This means the system is overloaded — slaves will experience unpredictable latency. The KTU examiner will reward the conclusion: **the baud rate must be increased to 1.5 Mbps, or the number of slaves per master reduced, to bring $T_{TR,total}$ below $T_{TTR}$.**

Recomputing at 1.5 Mbps:

$$T_{tx} = \frac{165}{1.5 \times 10^6} = 110 \text{ μs}$$

$$T_{master} = 20 \times 110 = 2200 \text{ μs} = 2.2 \text{ ms}$$

$$T_{TR,total} = 3 \times 2.2 = 6.6 \text{ ms} < 10 \text{ ms} \;\;\checkmark$$

---

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — PROFIBUS vs Other Fieldbuses

| Feature | PROFIBUS-DP | Foundation Fieldbus H1 | HART | Modbus RTU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Speed | 12 Mbps | 31.25 kbps | 1200 bps | 115.2 kbps |
| Medium | Twisted pair / Fiber | Twisted pair | 4–20 mA loop | RS-485 |
| Bus-powered | No (DP) / Yes (PA) | Yes | Yes | No |
| Intrinsic Safety | Yes (PA) | Yes | Yes | No |
| Max nodes | 126 | 32 | ~15 multi-drop | 247 |
| Determinism | Yes (token) | Yes (LAS) | No (poll) | No (poll) |
| Openness | Yes (PI) | Yes (FF) | Yes (HCF) | Yes (Modbus Org) |
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->

# SECTION 5 — KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1: **[KTU University Exam - May 2024]**
**Define PROFIBUS. List the three variants of PROFIBUS and state one key application of each.**

**Model Answer:**

PROFIBUS (Process Field Bus) is a vendor-independent, open fieldbus standard defined under IEC 61158/IEC 61784, used for real-time communication between controllers and field devices in industrial automation.

The three variants are:
- **PROFIBUS-DP (Decentralized Periphery):** Used in factory automation for high-speed communication with distributed I/O (sensors, actuators) at speeds up to 12 Mbps.
- **PROFIBUS-PA (Process Automation):** Used in process industries for intrinsically safe communication in hazardous (Ex) areas at 31.25 kbps, often bus-powered.
- **PROFIBUS-FMS (Fieldbus Message Specification):** Used (historically) for controller-to-controller communication at moderate speeds; largely obsolete.

---

### Question 2: **[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]**
**What is the role of the FDL (Fieldbus Data Link) layer in PROFIBUS? Mention the bus access method used.**

**Model Answer:**

The FDL (Layer 2) of PROFIBUS is responsible for:
- **Telegram framing** (start delimiter, addresses, data, frame check, end delimiter)
- **Error detection** (using parity and FCS)
- **Bus access control** through the **token passing** protocol among masters and **master-slave polling** for data exchange.

The bus access method is a **hybrid scheme**: the token circulates among active (Class 1) masters, and the master holding the token polls its assigned slaves one by one. This guarantees **deterministic, collision-free communication**.

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each)

### Question A (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam - May 2024 Model]**

**(a) [7 Marks]** Explain the PROFIBUS-DP telegram structure with a neat diagram. List the function of each field.

**(b) [7 Marks]** With a neat block diagram, explain the physical layer of PROFIBUS-DP and state the relationship between baud rate and maximum segment length.

#### Model Solution to (a) — Telegram Structure

A PROFIBUS-DP telegram consists of the following fields:

| Field | Length | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **SD** (Start Delimiter) | 1 byte | Marks the start of the telegram; varies by type (SD1, SD2, SD3, SD4) |
| **LE** (Length) | 1 byte | Specifies the length of the data unit (DA + SA + FC + DU) |
| **LEr** (Length Repeated) | 1 byte | Redundancy check on LE |
| **DA** (Destination Address) | 1 byte | Address of the receiver (0–127) |
| **SA** (Source Address) | 1 byte | Address of the sender |
| **FC** (Function Code) | 1 byte | Type of service (SRD, SDN, etc.) |
| **DU** (Data Unit) | 1–244 bytes | Payload — process data, parameters, diagnostics |
| **FCS** (Frame Check Sequence) | 1 byte | Cyclic redundancy over the telegram |
| **ED** (End Delimiter) | 1 byte | Marks the end of the telegram (always 0x16) |

**Header overhead** = 11 bytes (including padding and protocol bytes in DP-V0/DP-V1). The maximum telegram size is **255 bytes** total.

> The structure ensures that even with up to 244 bytes of user data, error detection (FCS) and addressing are preserved.

#### Model Solution to (b) — Physical Layer

The physical layer of PROFIBUS-DP uses **RS-485** differential signaling on a **shielded twisted pair** (Type A cable, purple sheath). The topology is a **linear bus** with **220 Ω terminating resistors** at each end to suppress reflections.

**Block Diagram of Physical Layer:**

```
[Master] ===Shielded Twisted Pair=== [Slave 1] -- [Slave 2] -- ... -- [Slave N]
   |                                                                 |
[220 Ω]                                                          [220 Ω]
```

**Key Parameters:**
- Differential voltage: ≥ 1.5 V (logic), ≤ 200 mV (idle)
- Maximum 32 stations per segment (up to 126 with 4 repeaters)

**Baud Rate vs Segment Length:**

| Baud Rate (kbps) | Max Length (m) |
|---|---|
| 9.6 – 93.75 | 1200 |
| 187.5 | 1000 |
| 500 | 400 |
| 1500 | 200 |
| 12 000 | 100 |

The relationship is **inversely proportional**: doubling the baud rate halves the maximum cable length, because higher frequencies suffer greater attenuation and signal distortion.

---

### Question B (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023 Model]**

**(a) [7 Marks]** Compare PROFIBUS-DP, PROFIBUS-PA, and PROFIBUS-FMS with respect to speed, application, physical layer, and intrinsic safety.

**(b) [7 Marks]** A PROFIBUS-DP network operates at 1.5 Mbps. A request telegram carries 8 bytes of data and the response carries 16 bytes of data. Header overhead is 11 bytes per telegram. Each byte is 11 bits (UART framing). Calculate the total request-response transmission time.

#### Model Solution to (a) — Comparison Table

| Feature | PROFIBUS-DP | PROFIBUS-PA | PROFIBUS-FMS |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Speed** | 9.6 kbps to 12 Mbps | Fixed 31.25 kbps | Up to 1.5 Mbps |
| **Application** | Factory automation, drives, I/O | Process industries, hazardous areas | Controller-to-controller (legacy) |
| **Physical Layer** | RS-485 / Fiber Optic | IEC 61158-2 Manchester | RS-485 |
| **Intrinsic Safety** | No (DP not IS) | **Yes** (IS-compliant) | No |
| **Bus-powered** | No | **Yes** (current from bus) | No |
| **Status** | Most widely used | Active in process plants | Obsolete |
| **Connection** | Direct | Via DP/PA coupler | Direct |

#### Model Solution to (b) — Transmission Time Calculation

**Step 1:** Total bytes in request telegram:
$$L_{req} = 11 + 8 = 19 \text{ bytes}$$

**Step 2:** Total bytes in response telegram:
$$L_{res} = 11 + 16 = 27 \text{ bytes}$$

**Step 3:** Total bits per telegram (UART framing, 11 bits/byte):
$$N_{bits,req} = 19 \times 11 = 209 \text{ bits}$$
$$N_{bits,res} = 27 \times 11 = 297 \text{ bits}$$

**Step 4:** Transmission time at $B = 1.5 \times 10^6$ bps:
$$T_{req} = \frac{209}{1.5 \times 10^6} = 1.393 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s} = 139.3 \text{ μs}$$

$$T_{res} = \frac{297}{1.5 \times 10^6} = 1.98 \times 10^{-4} \text{ s} = 198 \text{ μs}$$

**Step 5:** Total request-response time:
$$T_{total} = T_{req} + T_{res} = 139.3 + 198 = 337.3 \text{ μs}$$

> **Final Answer:** The total transaction time is approximately **337 μs** (≈ 0.34 ms), confirming that PROFIBUS-DP at 1.5 Mbps easily supports sub-millisecond cycle times for fast I/O scanning.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfalls — Where Students Lose Marks:**
> 1. **Forgetting the 11-bit UART framing** — Most students use 8 bits/byte in timing calculations. This is a 37.5% error and costs 2–3 marks.
> 2. **Confusing PROFIBUS-DP with PROFIBUS-PA** — DP is **not** intrinsically safe; PA is. Examiners deduct marks if you say "PROFIBUS supports IS."
> 3. **Omitting terminating resistors** — Any RS-485 PROFIBUS diagram without 220 Ω termination is incomplete.
> 4. **Wrong layer attribution** — Token passing is **Layer 2 (FDL)**, not Layer 1 or Layer 7. Examiners are strict about OSI mapping.
> 5. **Forgetting the address range** — Only 126 stations are usable (0 reserved, 127 broadcast), not 128.
> 6. **Confusing baud rate and bus cycle time** — They are inversely related. Students sometimes write "higher baud rate means longer cycle time" — this is **wrong**.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist for PROFIBUS (Module 2):**

- **PROFIBUS** = **PRO**cess **FI**eld **BUS** — IEC 61158 / IEC 61784 standard.
- **Three variants:** **DP** (fast, factory, 12 Mbps), **PA** (slow, process, IS-safe, 31.25 kbps), **FMS** (legacy controller-to-controller).
- **OSI layers used:** Layer 1 (Physical) + Layer 2 (FDL) + Layer 7 (Application). Layers 3–6 are skipped.
- **Bus access:** **Token passing** among active masters + **master-slave polling** for data exchange. Deterministic and collision-free.
- **Physical layer:** **RS-485** (DP/FMS) or **IEC 61158-2 Manchester** (PA) on shielded twisted pair.
- **Termination:** **220 Ω** resistors at both ends of each segment.
- **Max stations per segment:** **32**; with up to **4 repeaters** → **126 usable** (excluding address 0 service and 127 broadcast).
- **Baud rate vs length:** Inversely proportional — **9.6 kbps → 1200 m**; **12 Mbps → 100 m**.
- **Telegram structure:** SD, LE, LEr, DA, SA, FC, DU, FCS, ED — total **11 bytes overhead** + up to **244 bytes data**.
- **Bit framing:** 11 bits per byte (1 start + 8 data + 1 parity + 1 stop) → use this in all timing calculations.
- **Token time formulas:** $T_{tx} = \frac{11 \times (L_h + L_d)}{B}$; $T_{cycle} = \sum T_{TR,i} + T_{idle}$.
- **PA current limit:** ≤ 100 mA per segment (intrinsic safety).
- **DP/PA coupling:** Always via a **DP/PA coupler** or **PA link**; PA cannot be directly connected to DP masters.
- **FMS is obsolete** — replaced by **PROFINET (Industrial Ethernet)**.
- **Diagnostic services (DP-V1/V2):** Acyclic read/write of parameters, alarms, and isochronous real-time mode for motion control.
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->
